BIFURCATION OF MARITAL STATUS — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Jordan Alex Lee · Morgan Casey Lee

DECLARATION OF PARTIES AND PURPOSE OF THIS INFORMATION SHEET
This document concerns the marriage of Jordan Alex Lee and Morgan Casey Lee, married on June 14, 2015, in connection with a proceeding for dissolution of marriage contemplated in the California superior court for Sacramento County. It describes California's statutory procedure under Family Code § 2337 for requesting an early and separate trial on the sole issue of the dissolution of marital status — sometimes called "bifurcation" — apart from the remaining issues in a dissolution case, such as property division, support, and attorney's fees. It is a companion to this project's Petition for Dissolution of Marriage — Information Sheet, which describes the overall dissolution process; this document instead goes into the specific procedural mechanism for severing and trying the marital-status issue early, before the rest of the case is resolved. It is not itself a noticed motion, does not itself request or grant bifurcation, and does not dissolve, terminate, or otherwise change the marital status of Jordan Alex Lee and Morgan Casey Lee. Only a court order granting bifurcation, followed by a judgment on the status issue, can do that.

THE BIFURCATION MECHANISM: AN EARLY, SEPARATE TRIAL ON MARITAL STATUS
California Family Code § 2337 addresses a specific procedural mechanism available in a proceeding for dissolution of marriage: upon a noticed motion, the court may sever the issue of the dissolution of the marital status of the parties and grant an early and separate trial on that issue alone, apart from the other issues in the case. The statute's own language is permissive — the court "may" sever the status issue — meaning the decision whether to grant a request for bifurcation is committed to the court's discretion rather than being automatic upon a party's request. By its own terms, § 2337 is framed as applying in "a proceeding for dissolution of marriage." A judgment of legal separation does not itself terminate marital status (the parties remain married after a legal separation judgment), so this early-severance-of-status mechanism is specific to the dissolution process rather than to the separate legal-separation process described in this project's Petition for Legal Separation — Information Sheet.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "In a proceeding for dissolution of marriage, the court, upon noticed motion, may sever and grant an early and separate trial on the issue of the dissolution of the status of the marriage apart from other issues."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 2337(a) (California Legislative Information text), the discretionary noticed-motion mechanism for an early, separate trial on marital status (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=2337.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of a specific California procedural mechanism — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific marriage or dissolution, and not a claim about whether a court would grant bifurcation in any particular case. This is a single statutory subdivision (§ 2337(a)); no additional independent source was located for the core grant of authority itself (the practical-effect clause elsewhere in this document separately verifies related points using two independent California Court of Appeal decisions). The observation that a proceeding for legal separation does not terminate marital status is drawn from this corpus's own prior research on the legal-separation and dissolution statutes generally (reflected in this project's existing Family Law documents), not from a fresh, independently re-fetched quote captured specifically for this clause; it is offered here only to explain why § 2337 is described as a dissolution-specific mechanism, not as a full restatement of legal-separation law.

PRELIMINARY DECLARATION OF DISCLOSURE MUST ACCOMPANY THE MOTION
When a party files the noticed motion for bifurcation of marital status described elsewhere in this document, California law requires that a preliminary declaration of disclosure — together with a completed schedule of assets and debts — be served on the nonmoving party along with that motion. This requirement has two statutory exceptions: it does not apply if the preliminary declaration of disclosure has already been served previously, and it does not apply if the parties have stipulated in writing to defer service of the preliminary declaration of disclosure until a later time. This ties the bifurcation motion procedurally to California's general financial-disclosure framework in dissolution proceedings, rather than allowing the marital-status issue to be severed and tried before the parties have exchanged at least preliminary financial information (unless they have agreed in writing to defer it).

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "A preliminary declaration of disclosure with a completed schedule of assets and debts shall be served on the nonmoving party with the noticed motion unless it has been served previously, or unless the parties stipulate in writing to defer service of the preliminary declaration of disclosure until a later time."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 2337(b) (California Legislative Information text), the preliminary declaration of disclosure requirement and its two exceptions (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=2337.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of a specific California procedural requirement — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific marriage or dissolution, and not a claim about whether any specific document filed in a specific case satisfies this requirement. This is a single statutory subdivision (§ 2337(b)); no additional independent source was located for it. This clause does not describe the broader preliminary-declaration-of-disclosure requirements that apply to dissolution proceedings generally (what the schedule of assets and debts must contain, the separate final declaration of disclosure, or the consequences of nondisclosure) — it addresses only the specific timing rule tying that disclosure to a § 2337 bifurcation motion, not the general disclosure statutes themselves, which were not independently re-verified for this clause.

CONDITIONS A COURT MAY IMPOSE: INDEMNIFICATION FOR INSURANCE, TAX, AND RETIREMENT/SURVIVOR BENEFIT CONSEQUENCES
In granting a severance of the marital-status issue, California Family Code § 2337(c) authorizes — but does not require — the court to impose on the moving party any of a specific list of statutory conditions, and provides that an order imposing any of these conditions continues to bind that party's estate if the party dies. Among the conditions the statute lists: a party may be required to indemnify and hold the other party harmless for taxes, reassessments, interest, and penalties that would not have been payable had the parties still been married when the community estate was divided; to maintain the other party's and any minor children's existing health and medical insurance coverage (or provide comparable substitute coverage, or otherwise demonstrate the ability to pay for care that coverage would have covered) until judgment has been entered on all remaining issues and has become final; to indemnify the other party against loss of retirement, survivor, or deferred-compensation benefits — or associated elections or options — that the other party would have been entitled to as the spouse or surviving spouse of the party; and to indemnify the other party against loss of social security survivor benefits or elections the other party would have been entitled to as the surviving spouse of the party. Separately, § 2337(g) provides that if the party dies after entry of the judgment granting dissolution of marital status, any obligation imposed under this section remains enforceable against any asset — including its proceeds — against which the obligation would have been enforceable before the party's death.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "The court may impose upon a party any of the following conditions on granting a severance of the issue of the dissolution of the status of the marriage, and in case of that party’s death, an order of any of the following conditions continues to be binding upon that party’s estate:"
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 2337(c) (California Legislative Information text), the court's discretionary authority to impose conditions, binding on the party's estate (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=2337.)
  "The party shall indemnify and hold the other party harmless from any taxes, reassessments, interest, and penalties payable by the other party in connection with the division of the community estate that would not have been payable if the parties were still married at the time the division was made."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 2337(c)(1) (California Legislative Information text), the tax-consequence indemnification condition (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=2337.)
  "Until judgment has been entered on all remaining issues and has become final, the party shall maintain all existing health and medical insurance coverage for the other party and any minor children as named dependents, so long as the party is eligible to do so."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 2337(c)(2) (California Legislative Information text), the health and medical insurance coverage condition (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=2337.)
  "Until judgment has been entered on all remaining issues and has become final, the party shall indemnify and hold the other party harmless from any adverse consequences to the other party if the bifurcation results in the loss of the other party’s rights with respect to any retirement, survivor, or deferred compensation benefits under any plan, fund, or arrangement, or to any elections or options associated therewith, to the extent that the other party would have been entitled to those benefits or elections as the spouse or surviving spouse of the party."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 2337(c)(5) (California Legislative Information text), the retirement, survivor, and deferred-compensation benefits indemnification condition (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=2337.)
  "If the party dies after the entry of judgment granting a dissolution of marriage, any obligation imposed by this section shall be enforceable against any asset, including the proceeds thereof, against which these obligations would have been enforceable prior to the person’s death."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 2337(g) (California Legislative Information text), post-death enforceability of conditions imposed under this section (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=2337.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of a specific California procedural mechanism — not a claim about whether a court would impose any of these conditions in a specific case. All five citations in this clause are subsections of the same statutory section (§ 2337(c) and (g)), not independent sources of one another; they are quoted together because they state five distinct rules within one integrated conditions-and-enforcement scheme. Family Code § 2337(c) lists ten numbered categories of conditions in total; this clause describes only the indemnification-style conditions in paragraphs (1), (2), (5), and (6) (tax consequences, health insurance, retirement/survivor/deferred-compensation benefits, and social security benefits). It does not describe paragraph (3) (probate homestead rights), paragraph (4) (probate family allowance rights), paragraph (7) (beneficiary-designation orders for certain nonprobate transfers under the Probate Code), or paragraph (8) (orders concerning IRA distribution deferral) — those paragraphs were fetched as part of the same primary-source text but are not restated or quoted here. The security-interest and bond-related conditions in paragraph (9), and the general catchall in paragraph (10), are addressed in a separate clause of this document.

CONDITIONS A COURT MAY IMPOSE: SECURITY INTERESTS, BONDS, AND OTHER UNDERTAKINGS
Beyond the indemnification obligations described elsewhere in this document, California Family Code § 2337(c)(9) separately authorizes the court, upon a showing that circumstances exist that would place a substantial burden on enforcing either party's community property rights — or would eliminate the surviving party's ability to enforce those rights if the other party died before the community property was divided, distributed, or paid as ordered — to order a specific security interest designed to reduce or eliminate the likelihood that a postmortem enforcement proceeding would be ineffective or unduly burdensome to the surviving party. The statute lists, among the forms such an order may take, an order that the party provide an undertaking (a bond), and an order to provide a security interest by Qualified Domestic Relations Order from that party's share of a retirement plan or plans. Separately, § 2337(c)(10) allows the court to impose, as a condition of severance, any other condition the court determines is just and equitable — a catchall beyond the specifically enumerated conditions in the rest of the subdivision.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "Upon a showing that circumstances exist that would place a substantial burden of enforcement upon either party’s community property rights or would eliminate the ability of the surviving party to enforce his or her community property rights if the other party died before the division and distribution or compliance with any court-ordered payment of any community property interest therein, including, but not limited to, a situation in which preemption under federal law applies to an asset of a party, or purchase by a bona fide purchaser has occurred, the court may order a specific security interest designed to reduce or eliminate the likelihood that a postmortem enforcement proceeding would be ineffective or unduly burdensome to the surviving party."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 2337(c)(9) (California Legislative Information text), the showing required, and the court's authority to order a specific security interest (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=2337.)
  "An order that the party provide an undertaking."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 2337(c)(9)(A) (California Legislative Information text), an order that the party provide an undertaking (a bond) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=2337.)
  "An order to provide a security interest by Qualified Domestic Relations Order from that party’s share of a retirement plan or plans."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 2337(c)(9)(B) (California Legislative Information text), a security interest by Qualified Domestic Relations Order (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=2337.)
  "Any other condition the court determines is just and equitable."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 2337(c)(10) (California Legislative Information text), the general catchall condition (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=2337.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of a specific California procedural mechanism — not a claim about whether a court would order a bond or other security interest in a specific case. All four citations in this clause are subsections of the same statutory section (§ 2337(c)(9)-(10)), not independent sources of one another. Paragraph (9) itself lists several additional forms of order this document does not separately quote (for example, an order for the creation of a trust, or other reasonably necessary arrangements), and cross-references its own exceptions for certain nonprobate transfers not created by either party, irrevocable trusts, and similar circumstances (§ 2337(c)(9)(B)) that this clause does not restate.

MANDATORY PRE-JUDGMENT STEPS FOR RETIREMENT PLANS
Unlike the discretionary conditions described elsewhere in this document, California Family Code § 2337(d) imposes mandatory steps tied specifically to retirement and pension plans that must occur prior to, or simultaneously with, entry of judgment granting dissolution of the status of the marriage. First, the party's retirement or pension plan must be joined as a party to the dissolution proceeding, unless joinder is precluded or made unnecessary by Title 1 of the federal Employee Retirement Income Security Act of 1974 (ERISA) or other applicable law. Second, to preserve each spouse's claims in all retirement plan benefits, the court must enter — for each retirement plan in which either party is a participant, in connection with the status judgment — one of three things: an order under Family Code § 2610 disposing of each party's interest in the retirement plan benefits, including survivor and death benefits; an interim order preserving the nonemployee party's right to those benefits, including survivor and death benefits, pending entry of judgment on the remaining issues; or a specified statutory attachment to the status judgment that provisionally awards each party a one-half interest in benefits accrued during the marriage and continues the parties' treatment as married for survivor-benefit purposes to that extent, pending further order. Family Code § 2337(e) further requires the moving party to promptly serve a copy of any such order, interim order, or attachment, together with a copy of the status judgment, on the retirement or pension plan administrator.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "Prior to, or simultaneously with, entry of judgment granting dissolution of the status of the marriage, all of the following shall occur:"
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 2337(d) (California Legislative Information text), the timing requirement for retirement-plan-related steps (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=2337.)
  "The party’s retirement or pension plan shall be joined as a party to the proceeding for dissolution, unless joinder is precluded or made unnecessary by Title 1 of the federal Employee Retirement Income Security Act of 1974 (29 U.S.C. Sec. 1001 et seq.), as amended (ERISA), or any other applicable law."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 2337(d)(1) (California Legislative Information text), mandatory joinder of the retirement or pension plan (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=2337.)
  "To preserve the claims of each spouse in all retirement plan benefits upon entry of judgment granting a dissolution of the status of the marriage, the court shall enter one of the following in connection with the judgment for each retirement plan in which either party is a participant:"
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 2337(d)(2) (California Legislative Information text), the requirement to enter one of three protective orders for each retirement plan (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=2337.)
  "An interim order preserving the nonemployee party’s right to retirement plan benefits, including survivor and death benefits, pending entry of judgment on all remaining issues."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 2337(d)(2)(B) (California Legislative Information text), the interim-order option preserving retirement plan benefits (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=2337.)
  "The moving party shall promptly serve a copy of any order, interim order, or attachment entered pursuant to paragraph (2) of subdivision (d), and a copy of the judgment granting a dissolution of the status of the marriage, on the retirement or pension plan administrator."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 2337(e) (California Legislative Information text), the moving party's obligation to serve the retirement plan administrator (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=2337.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of a specific California procedural mechanism — not a claim about whether any specific retirement plan would in fact be joined, or which of the three protective mechanisms a court would select, in a specific case. All citations in this clause are subsections of the same statutory section (§ 2337(d)-(e)), not independent sources of one another. This clause does not independently verify the substantive content of the cross-referenced Family Code § 2610 (governing orders dividing retirement plan benefits) — it is cited here only as the first of three named options under § 2337(d)(2), not re-verified in its own right. The statutory attachment language quoted in part is a fixed, capitalized form of words the statute itself prescribes for use in the judgment; this clause paraphrases its general effect rather than reproducing it in full.

EFFECT ON MARITAL STATUS: RESERVED JURISDICTION AND THE END OF THE MARRIAGE
California Family Code § 2337(f) requires that a judgment granting dissolution of the status of the marriage expressly reserve jurisdiction for later determination of all other pending issues in the case — meaning a status judgment under this section does not itself resolve property division, support, attorney's fees, or other remaining issues; those continue to be litigated in the same proceeding after the status judgment is entered. California appellate decisions describe the practical effect of such a judgment on the parties themselves. In In re Marriage of Turfe (2018) 23 Cal.App.5th 1118, the Court of Appeal described a husband's status-only dissolution judgment as one that terminated his marriage to his wife and reserved jurisdiction over all other issues, and separately noted that a "status only" dissolution judgment is immediately appealable as a final judgment on the issue of dissolution of marital status, citing Family Code § 2337(a). And in In re Marriage of Fink (1976) 54 Cal.App.3d 357 — the decision that established the bifurcated-trial procedure the Legislature later codified in § 2337 — the Court of Appeal observed that, because the wife's appeal of a status-only judgment remained pending, the husband had been unable to secure his final decree and freedom to remarry, reflecting that once such a judgment becomes final, the party regains the freedom to remarry notwithstanding that the remaining issues in the case are still being litigated.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "A judgment granting a dissolution of the status of the marriage shall expressly reserve jurisdiction for later determination of all other pending issues."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 2337(f) (California Legislative Information text), the requirement that a status judgment expressly reserve jurisdiction over remaining issues (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=2337.)
  "Robert Turfe (husband) appeals a judgment of dissolution of marriage as to status only. The judgment terminated his marriage to Summer Turfe (wife) and reserved jurisdiction over all other issues."
  — In re Marriage of Turfe (2018) 23 Cal.App.5th 1118 (opinion text via CourtListener), the practical effect of a status-only dissolution judgment on the parties (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/6239655/turfe-v-turfe-in-re-turfe/)
  "A "status only" dissolution judgment is immediately appealable as a final judgment on the issue of dissolution of marital status. (Fam. Code, § 2337, subd. (a) [early and separate trial on dissolution of marital status]"
  — In re Marriage of Turfe (2018) 23 Cal.App.5th 1118, footnote 1 (opinion text via CourtListener), confirming a status-only judgment is immediately appealable under Family Code § 2337(a) (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/6239655/turfe-v-turfe-in-re-turfe/)
  "In the case at bench, due to wife’s appeal, husband has been unable to secure his final decree and freedom to remarry."
  — In re Marriage of Fink (1976) 54 Cal.App.3d 357, 367 (opinion text via CourtListener), freedom to remarry following a final status judgment (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/2139092/in-re-marriage-of-fink/)
  Known gap: These are two genuinely independent California Court of Appeal decisions (Turfe, decided in 2018 by California's Second Appellate District, and Fink, decided in 1976 by California's Second Appellate District in an earlier era of that same court, applying the predecessor Family Law Act) — not two subsections of the same statute — so they are independent of one another and of the statutory citation in this clause. Fink predates the 1994 recodification that created the current Family Code and today's § 2337; it was decided under the former Civil Code framework and used the term "final decree" rather than today's "judgment," but the current Turfe opinion cites Fink for the closely related proposition that a status-only judgment is immediately appealable under current § 2337(a), which is why it is treated here as continuing, on-point authority. Neither case, and no statutory text located in this document's research, states as an abstract, generally applicable rule that marital status is restored, or that a party becomes free to remarry, at any specific, universally applicable moment (for example, immediately upon the trial court's ruling versus only once that ruling becomes final and unappealable); Fink's "freedom to remarry" statement arises from the specific procedural posture of that case — a pending appeal delaying finality — rather than from a freestanding statutory holding, and Family Code § 2337 itself never uses the word "remarry." This clause's statutory citation (§ 2337(f)) concerns only the reserved-jurisdiction requirement; the remarriage point rests on these two cases rather than on statutory text.

SIGNATURE AND ACKNOWLEDGMENT — NOT A COURT FILING
I declare under penalty of perjury under the laws of the State of California that the foregoing background information is true and correct.

Executed on September 1, 2026 at Oakland, California.

Signature of Jordan Alex Lee: ☐ _________________________

[This information sheet is prepared for use alongside an actual noticed motion for bifurcation of marital status that would be filed in a pending California dissolution proceeding. It does not itself constitute, replace, or complete that motion, and it does not sever any issue, grant an early trial, or dissolve, terminate, or otherwise change the marital status of Jordan Alex Lee and Morgan Casey Lee; only a court order and subsequent judgment can do that.]

expectedJSON.body: Beyond the indemnification obligations described elsewhere in this document, California Family Code § 2337(c)(9) separately authorizes the court, upon a showing that circumstances exist that would place a substantial burden on enforcing either party's community property rights — or would eliminate the surviving party's ability to enforce those rights if the other party died before the community property was divided, distributed, or paid as ordered — to order a specific security interest designed to reduce or eliminate the likelihood that a postmortem enforcement proceeding would be ineffective or unduly burdensome to the surviving party. The statute lists, among the forms such an order may take, an order that the party provide an undertaking (a bond), and an order to provide a security interest by Qualified Domestic Relations Order from that party's share of a retirement plan or plans. Separately, § 2337(c)(10) allows the court to impose, as a condition of severance, any other condition the court determines is just and equitable — a catchall beyond the specifically enumerated conditions in the rest of the subdivision.

expectedJSON.body: Unlike the discretionary conditions described elsewhere in this document, California Family Code § 2337(d) imposes mandatory steps tied specifically to retirement and pension plans that must occur prior to, or simultaneously with, entry of judgment granting dissolution of the status of the marriage. First, the party's retirement or pension plan must be joined as a party to the dissolution proceeding, unless joinder is precluded or made unnecessary by Title 1 of the federal Employee Retirement Income Security Act of 1974 (ERISA) or other applicable law. Second, to preserve each spouse's claims in all retirement plan benefits, the court must enter — for each retirement plan in which either party is a participant, in connection with the status judgment — one of three things: an order under Family Code § 2610 disposing of each party's interest in the retirement plan benefits, including survivor and death benefits; an interim order preserving the nonemployee party's right to those benefits, including survivor and death benefits, pending entry of judgment on the remaining issues; or a specified statutory attachment to the status judgment that provisionally awards each party a one-half interest in benefits accrued during the marriage and continues the parties' treatment as married for survivor-benefit purposes to that extent, pending further order. Family Code § 2337(e) further requires the moving party to promptly serve a copy of any such order, interim order, or attachment, together with a copy of the status judgment, on the retirement or pension plan administrator.

expectedJSON.body: California Family Code § 2337(f) requires that a judgment granting dissolution of the status of the marriage expressly reserve jurisdiction for later determination of all other pending issues in the case — meaning a status judgment under this section does not itself resolve property division, support, attorney's fees, or other remaining issues; those continue to be litigated in the same proceeding after the status judgment is entered. California appellate decisions describe the practical effect of such a judgment on the parties themselves. In In re Marriage of Turfe (2018) 23 Cal.App.5th 1118, the Court of Appeal described a husband's status-only dissolution judgment as one that terminated his marriage to his wife and reserved jurisdiction over all other issues, and separately noted that a "status only" dissolution judgment is immediately appealable as a final judgment on the issue of dissolution of marital status, citing Family Code § 2337(a). And in In re Marriage of Fink (1976) 54 Cal.App.3d 357 — the decision that established the bifurcated-trial procedure the Legislature later codified in § 2337 — the Court of Appeal observed that, because the wife's appeal of a status-only judgment remained pending, the husband had been unable to secure his final decree and freedom to remarry, reflecting that once such a judgment becomes final, the party regains the freedom to remarry notwithstanding that the remaining issues in the case are still being litigated.

expectedJSON.gap: These are two genuinely independent California Court of Appeal decisions (Turfe, decided in 2018 by California's Second Appellate District, and Fink, decided in 1976 by California's Second Appellate District in an earlier era of that same court, applying the predecessor Family Law Act) — not two subsections of the same statute — so they are independent of one another and of the statutory citation in this clause. Fink predates the 1994 recodification that created the current Family Code and today's § 2337; it was decided under the former Civil Code framework and used the term "final decree" rather than today's "judgment," but the current Turfe opinion cites Fink for the closely related proposition that a status-only judgment is immediately appealable under current § 2337(a), which is why it is treated here as continuing, on-point authority. Neither case, and no statutory text located in this document's research, states as an abstract, generally applicable rule that marital status is restored, or that a party becomes free to remarry, at any specific, universally applicable moment (for example, immediately upon the trial court's ruling versus only once that ruling becomes final and unappealable); Fink's "freedom to remarry" statement arises from the specific procedural posture of that case — a pending appeal delaying finality — rather than from a freestanding statutory holding, and Family Code § 2337 itself never uses the word "remarry." This clause's statutory citation (§ 2337(f)) concerns only the reserved-jurisdiction requirement; the remarriage point rests on these two cases rather than on statutory text.
